evidence.snippet: These data provide the first evidence that CHMP4B, which encodes a key component of the endosome sorting complex required for the transport-III (ESCRT-III) system of mammalian cells, plays a vital role in the maintenance of lens transparency.

nodes.description: A heterozygous missense substitution alters a conserved residue of the ESCRT-III subunit CHMP4B (D129V, E161K, H57R and S196C lie in the SNF7 domain). CHMP4 proteins polymerize into spiral filaments that bend membranes away from the cytoplasm before scission. Chmp4b is expressed in lens epithelial cells and elongating fiber cells at the lens equator. Homozygous D129V knock-in mouse embryos survive longer than null embryos, suggesting the V allele retains some function; transfection data were read as a deleterious gain of function. Whether human alleles act by dominant interference, gain of function or partial loss is not settled.

nodes.description: Wild-type CHMP4B localizes to chromosome bridges and micronuclei, which are flanked by lysosomal and autophagic markers, including in a human lens epithelial cell line. Full-length D129V-CHMP4B colocalizes with these structures in fewer transfected HeLa cells than wild type. The proposed consequence, impaired autophagolysosomal clearance of extranuclear chromatin during lens fiber differentiation, has not been tested in lens tissue.

evidence.snippet: First, a truncated form of recombinant CHMP4B harboring the p.D129V substitution (D129V-CHMP4B1–150) displayed a different sub-cellular localization pattern to wild-type (CHMP4B1–150) and a reduced (~ 50%) capacity to release virus-like-particles (HIV-1 Gag polyprotein, Pr55) from the cell surface - consistent with deleterious effects on the endosome-lysosome pathway (Shiels et al., 2007).

nodes.description: Lens-specific Chmp4b knockdown in mice disturbs fiber cell organization at birth, with large vesicle-like structures, fiber cell degeneration, lens cell death and, in severe cases, lens ablation. Heterozygous loss does not cause cataract in mice, so the relevance of this node to the dominant human disease rests on the assumption that the human alleles reduce or interfere with CHMP4B function in fiber cells.
